title: Get Up, Stand Up
author: Make Work Better
summary: The piece opens by dismissing the common conference-circuit advice to 'just go for a walk' as an inadequate answer to systemic workplace burnout, then pivots to genuinely engage with Manoush Zomorodi's research on desk-bound work. Zomorodi found that hourly five-minute walks improved her own blood sugar, blood pressure, and mood, and a 20,000-person study of the same intervention found meaningful drops in fatigue and gains in productivity. The author frames this through Zomorodi's concept of 'screen apnea' — shallow breathing induced by prolonged screen focus. The actual argument is more measured than a simple endorsement: getting up and moving is real and worth prioritizing, but it cannot substitute for addressing the structural, adrenaline-driven culture that makes people feel they can't step away in the first place.
points: A single speaker's 'just go for a walk' advice for burnout is only half right: walking has a real, measurable effect, but it cannot fix a workplace culture that runs on adrenaline.
Zomorodi's own five-minute-per-hour walking experiment produced a 42% improvement in blood sugar and a five-point blood pressure drop.
A 20,000-person replication of the same hourly-walk intervention found a 25% drop in reported fatigue alongside marked productivity gains.
'Screen apnea' — shallow breathing brought on by prolonged screen focus — is presented as a physiological cost of desk work distinct from mental fatigue.
The sedentary share of the workday rose from roughly 25% in 1950 to over 80% by 2019, reframing 'sit less' as a response to a genuinely new historical condition.
quotes: Six years of experience of self medicating with a few thousand steps has taught us that walking alone isn't enough to solve the problem of endemic workplace stress.
The issue is that we're all looking for push-button solutions to systemic problems. When it comes to fixing work we're seeking answers that are easy, immediate and individual.
She's clear on the size of the challenge of contemporary work, 'in 1950, 25% of the workday was sedentary. By 2019 it was over 80%.'

Having seen big personal gains, she signed up twenty thousand participants in a scaled exploration of these actions. Participants reported fatigue dropping 25%, productivity also showed marked improvements.
Zomorodi has framed some of the issue as 'screen apnea' saying that sitting and staring at a screen causes shallow breathing.

While I don't think getting up and walking is going to fix burnout, we do need to address the current sedentary state of work. The evidence for getting up from our desk is real and has effect sizes far beyond what we might guess.
